newsitem.title: USA: Bell Atlantic sees early entry into long-distance.
newsitem.headline: Bell Atlantic sees early entry into long-distance.

text.p: Bell Atlantic Corp., which completed its merger with Nynex Corp. on Thursday, said it expects to be the first Baby Bell local telephone company to be allowed to enter the long-distance phone business.
Bell Atlantic executives said Friday it has a headstart on other Baby Bells to gain regulatory approval for long-distance phone service in its 12-state local calling region.
"The big issue for us is moving into long-distance," said Ivan Seidenberg, the company's vice-chairman, president and chief operating officer, told reporters at a news conference.
"We aim to capture at least 25 percent of the long distance market in our region over the next five years," he said earlier in a prepared statement.

The combined company now dominates local phone service along the Eastern seaboard of the United States from Maine to Virginia but faces growing competition as efforts to open local phone markets to competition take hold.
"We think we will be in long distance very soon," Bell Atlantic Chairman Raymond Smith said.
The officials also said management succession plans and projected cost savings from the $25.6 billion merger remain in line with what the company set forth when it struck the deal 16 months ago.

The company has said it expected the merger to result in annualized savings in the range of $850 million to $900 million a year over time from combined capital spending, lower operating costs and job cuts to eliminate duplication.
"We have plans for the savings we will achieve this year and they are on track with what Wall Street has been estimating," Seidenberg said.
On Thursday, the Federal Communications Commission announced its approval of the merger, the final regulatory hurdle before the deal could become effective.
With $27.8 billion in revenues and $11.5 billion in net income, the merged Bell Atlantic is the second-largest communications company in America after AT&T Corp.
It provides 37 million lines to its 26 million domestic phone customers and has another 3.4 million wireless customers in the region. The company will be based in New York City.

Responding to reporters' questions, Bell Atlantic executives said they believed the conditions agreed to with the FCC to gain approval for the merger gave the company "a head up" on long-distance entry.
The voluntary commitments it made to the FCC are designed to reduce Bell Atlantic's dominance over local phone service on the East Coast.
Regulators want to get rid of barriers to competition in local markets before they allow Bell Atlantic to enter the long-distance service.
Bell Atlantic said it has no plans to use the courts to win long-distance entry, a tactic pursued by Baby Bells SBC Communications Inc. and Ameritech Corp. .
Discussing the executive succession plans for the company, Ray Smith brushed aside speculation that he may have reservations about making Seidenberg his successor as planned.
"Ivan is my candidate," Smith said. "He is the person the board has accepted."
Seidenberg added the succession is now "the board's responsibility."
Seidenberg, the former chief executive of Nynex, is slated to take over from Smith as chief executive by August 1998, and as chairman upon Smith's retirement at the end of 1998.
Bell Atlantic provides 37 million lines to its 26 million domestic phone customers and has another 3.4 million wireless customers in the region. The company will be based in New York City.
Bell Atlantic fell 50 cents to $75.44 on the New York Stock Exchange.
